newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine leftist opposition to APEC grows.
newsitem.headline: Philippine leftist opposition to APEC grows.

text.p: Philippine security forces stepped up preparations on Sunday to safeguard Asia-Pacific leaders as opposition to their November 25 summit meeting intensified, mainly among left-wing groups.
Police and soldiers held full-scale dress rehearsals in Manila from the early hours of Sunday, practising how to tackle everything from a terrorist kidnapping bid to accidental fires.
The Philippines has assembled a security force of 30,000, including the police and the military, for the meeting. The security budget is estimated at US $3.5 million.
"The security people will leave no stone unturned to protect not just the leaders but all of those attending APEC," Press Undersecretary Honesto Isleta told Reuters.
The government has already come under fire for security preparations, especially its ban on East Timor independence leader and Nobel Peace laureate Jose Ramos-Horta.
Immigration officials have also refused visas to six delegates to a leftist "Peasants' Summit", which opened in Manila on Sunday.
Security chiefs have declined to say if there have been any direct threat to U.S. President Bill Clinton or other leaders due to attend the summit of the 18-member regional group.
But one senior official who declined to be named said the chief concern was mainly leftist groups seeking to disrupt APEC as a way to embarrass the Philippine government.
The government fears that terrorists could take advantage of any confusion caused by leftist protests to stage attacks.
The official said anti-APEC groups were fomenting unrest among labour unions linked to the summit and the ministerial meeting that precedes it on November 22-23.
The official declined to give details but Manila newspapers have reported unrest among workers in the hotel, transport, power and telecommunications sectors, all of which play a key role in APEC.
Employees have threatened to go on strike at the Manila Hotel, where Clinton, Indonesia's President Suharto and the Sultan of Brunei are due to stay.
They said in a petition to the Department of Labour that the strike is over management's failure to agree on a new employment package.

The Philippines had a strong leftist movement that fought an armed insurrection for decades. That insurgency has largely ended and the left weakened both by internecine feuding and growing prosperity under President Fidel Ramos's government.
The Philippines hopes to use its role as this year's APEC host to showcase what economists agree is a dramatic economic revival after years of stagnation.
This revival has largely been credited to President Ramos's wide-ranging economic reforms, which are the kind of liberalisation measures APEC is designed to promote.
But opponents argue that trade liberalisation benefits only big business while the poor, especially in farm areas, suffer.
The "Peasants' Summit" in Manila is designed to highlight the plight of small farmers in an era of increasingly freer trade, organisers said in a statement.
The meeting is the first in a series of events by anti-APEC groups that also includes a "parallel summit" and a protest motorcade from Manila to Subic.
